label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
**About the house in Glenmore**

I've started this post four times. Each time I either sound like I'm reading out the minutes of a parish meeting or I go on about the light over the lake for a page and a half. So I'll just tell you plainly, the way I should have done in the first place.

I have agreed to sell the house in Glenmore. The sale was agreed on the 3rd of November and it closes on the 15th of January. I'm putting the date at the top so nobody hears it from someone else, because some of you already heard the news that way. That was my fault and I'll come back to it.

For those in Boston and Perth and Leeds who haven't been out there in a while, or the younger ones who were only small, this is the old Mulkerrin place outside Oughterard. Tom's grandfather, Pádraig Mulkerrin, built it in 1931. Tom grew up in it. Most of you have eaten a dinner in that kitchen at some point, or been sent out to the haggard to get something you couldn't find, or been told to close the gate after you.

I want to explain why I've done it. I'm not trying to talk anyone round. I'd just rather you had the whole of it from me than bits and pieces over the phone.

**Since Tom**

Tom died in March of 2024. Most of you know that, and a lot of you were at the funeral or rang or wrote, and I've never properly thanked you all for that. Thank you.

Since then I've been driving out to Glenmore every second week. It's forty minutes each way from me. I open the windows, light the range if it's cold, run the taps, check the pipes, look at the ceilings for new stains, and generally walk around the place making sure it's still standing. Then I lock up and drive home. In the beginning I didn't mind it at all. I wanted to go. It was somewhere I could be with him, if that makes sense. I'd sit at the table with a cup of tea and not do much of anything.

But a house that nobody lives in goes downhill quicker than you'd believe. It needs people in it, fires lit, doors opening and closing. Without that the damp gets in and stays. I could see it happening and I couldn't keep up with it, coming once a fortnight with a bucket and a mop.

**The roof and the rest of it**

In September I had Ó Flaithearta's out to look at the roof, because I knew some of the slates had gone and I was worried about the back chimney. Their quote came to €38,000 for the slates and the chimney. On top of that there's damp in the back bedroom that's been getting worse, and that'll need its own fixing. The septic tank also has to be replaced, and that has to be done to sell to anyone at all, so there was never any getting around it.

I'm not telling you the figures to make it sound like I had no choice. I could have found a way. People do. But when I sat down with the quote I had to ask myself honestly what I'd be spending it on. Would it be a house somebody was going to live in, or a house I'd keep driving out to on my own, airing rooms nobody sleeps in? I didn't like the answer, but I knew it.

**The step at the back door**

This next part I've told nobody until now, so I'm sorry to be telling you on a blog. It's the reason I can't keep putting it off.

Last February, on one of my fortnightly visits, there was frost on the step at the back door and I went down on it. I don't know how long it took me to get up exactly, but I think it was about twenty minutes. Nothing was broken, thank God. I was sore for a good while after and I had a bruise on my hip the size of a saucer. But I lay there on the cold step looking up at the sky and there wasn't a soul for miles who knew I was there. My phone was in my bag on the kitchen table.

I got up eventually and drove home and didn't tell anyone. Partly I was embarrassed. Partly I knew that if I said it out loud I'd have to do something about it, and I wasn't ready.

I'm telling you now because it's part of the truth. Since that morning I've been afraid out there on my own. I still went, every second week, but I'd be listening to every creak and I'd walk across that yard like an old woman, which I suppose I am. I'm seventy-one. I can't go on maintaining that house by myself, and I don't want to be found on the back step some winter by the postman.

**Who's buying it**

The buyers are a young couple called Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, so he's from just up the road really. They have two small children. They want to live in it. It will be their home, not a holiday let or something to do up and sell on.

In the summer there was an offer from a couple in Dublin, and it was higher than the Joyces'. I took the lower one on purpose. I'm not saying that to sound noble. The Joyces' price was fair, and I've no complaints. But when I met them and saw the two children running around the yard, and Kevin asking about the lake and whether the field at the back floods, I knew which one Tom would have wanted.

Tom always said that house should have children in it and not be a museum. He said it about his own mother's front room, which nobody was allowed to sit in, and he said it again when we used to talk, half joking, about what would happen to the place when we were gone. I didn't think I'd be the one deciding it. But I heard him say it more than once, and I believe he meant it.

**What's being kept**

I know that for some of you the worry will be about the things in it, so I want to be clear about what's staying in the family.

- The dresser is going to Úna.
- Pádraig's fiddle is being kept.
- All the photographs are being kept. I'll sort through them over the winter. If anyone wants copies of particular ones, tell me and we'll work something out.
- The Sacred Heart lamp is coming with me.
- The gate sign is being kept too.

If there's something else you have a particular memory of, a chair or a picture or whatever it is, please tell me before the house is cleared and I'll do my best. I'd rather be asked than have someone find out afterwards that it's gone.

The Joyces have also said, without me even asking, that the family is welcome to come out and walk the land any time. I believe they mean it. So the lake will still be there, and the haggard, and the view from the top field, and you'll be able to go and stand in them.

**The haggard, and the lake**

I'll allow myself a bit of remembering here, and then I'll get on with it.

Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind that house in 1979. It was raining, of course. It was always raining. The cattle were standing at the wall watching us like a jury. He'd been working himself up to it all afternoon and I knew something was wrong with him, because he wouldn't sit still. Then he just came out with it beside the hay, both of us soaked. I said yes and one of the cows lowed, and we laughed so much we had to hold on to each other. That's the honest truth of it.

Later on, the children learned to swim in the lake below the house. Every summer we'd bring them down, and the water was freezing even in July. Declan wouldn't come out. He'd be blue in the lips and shaking and still saying "five more minutes." I used to stand on the bank with the towel held out like a matador, threatening him. He was always the one who wanted to stay longest.

I know those memories are tied up with the place for every one of you, in your own ways. They are for me too. But over the best part of two years, driving out there and back, I've come to realise that I can keep Tom's memory without keeping the house. I didn't believe that at the start. I do now. He isn't in the slates or the septic tank. He's in the fact that I can still see him in that haggard in the rain with his hair stuck to his forehead. I'll have that wherever I'm living.

**How you found out**

Now the part I'm least proud of.

Some of you heard about the sale second-hand, before I'd told you myself. I meant to tell everyone properly. I kept waiting for the right time, or for when I'd have the words, and in the meantime word got around, the way it does. That's on me. It shouldn't have happened, and I'm sorry for it.

I want to be clear about what I'm apologising for. I'm sorry for how you found out. I'm not sorry for the decision. I've thought about it more than anything since Tom died, and I believe it's right. But you deserved to hear it from me first, and some of you didn't, and I can't undo that.

**Declan**

Declan, I know you read these, so this part is for you, though everyone else is going to read it too, and I think that's alright.

You heard it from Gráinne on a WhatsApp, not from me. You shouldn't have. You rang me at two in the morning your time, and I could hear how upset you were. You said I was selling Dad. I said things back to you that I shouldn't have said, and I've been sorry about them every day since. I was tired and hurt and I got defensive, and I took it out on you. You didn't deserve that.

I regret not talking it over with you before I agreed anything. I should have. You're his son and that house meant a great deal to you, and I know you have your own picture of it and your own memories that I'm not part of. I should have rung you myself, long before any of this got as far as it did.

I want to be honest with you about the other side of it too, because I think you'd rather that than me saying what you want to hear. I wasn't willing to wait until your summer visit. I know that's what you'd have wanted, for us to walk around it together and talk it all through. But that would have meant another winter out there on my own, with the roof the way it is and the step the way it is, and after February I couldn't face that. I don't think I could have explained that properly to you on the phone, because I hadn't told anyone about the fall. Maybe if I had, it would have made more sense.

I'm not selling your Dad, love. I know that's not really what you meant, or not all of it. I think you meant that it feels like he's being taken away again. I understand that, because it felt that way to me too for a long time. But he's not in the house. He's in you, in your stubbornness and your blue lips in the lake and the way you'd stay out in the water long after everyone else had given up. I see him in you all the time.

I'm not angry with you. I want to say that plainly so there's no doubt about it. I'm not angry. The door is open, and the phone is on, at any hour, even two in the morning. Whenever you want to talk, I'll be here, and if you'd rather not talk for a while, I'll still be here.

**Sunday the 13th of December**

Before the house is cleared I'd like us to have one last day out there together, as many of us as can manage it.

The plan is Sunday the 13th of December. I'll have soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies, because the haggard will be a swamp and you know it. Come and walk around, go down to the lake, go up the top field, take photographs, take a stone from the wall if you want one. Bring the children so they can see where their grandfather or their great-uncle grew up. If there's something in the house you'd like, that'll be a good day to tell me.

I know a lot of you are too far away to come, and I understand that completely. If you can't come but want to see it, tell me and I'll get someone to do a video call from the kitchen, or take pictures of whatever you want to see. If there's a particular corner of the place you'd like photographed, just say.

If you can come, let me know roughly how many, so I make enough soup. Last time I underestimated this family I ran out of bread in half an hour.

**That's it**

I think that's everything. I've tried to be honest about all of it, the parts I'm sure about and the parts I made a mess of. The sale is agreed. It closes on the 15th of January. The Joyces are a good young family and they'll fill the place with noise, the way Tom wanted. The dresser and the fiddle and the photographs and the lamp and the gate sign are staying with us. You're all welcome on the land whenever you want to go. And on the 13th of December there'll be soup.

Thank you for reading this far. Thank you to Úna for setting this blog up all those years ago, because I don't think I could have said all this on the phone one by one without making a hames of it.

With love to you all, near and far,
